DEPARTMENT 731 LAW AND MOTION RULINGS

[TENTATIVE] ORDER RE: PLAINTIFF MICHAEL BRIAN SMITH’S MOTION TO SET ASIDE/VACATE JUDGMENT [CRS #8855] Dept. 731 8:30 a.m. July 21, 2026

Moving Party: Plaintiff, Michael Brian Smith

Opposing Party: Defendant, Michael Kors Inc.

Notice: OK

Plaintiff Michael B. Smith brought this suit against his former employer, Defendant Michael Kors Inc., alleging race discrimination in his employment and a subsequent unlawful layoff.

On March 26, 2026, the Court granted a motion for judgment on the pleadings filed by Defendant, which disposed of the then-operative March 19, 2024, Second Amended Complaint (“SAC”). Plaintiff filed a motion for reconsideration on March 30, 2026, which was opposed by Defendant, and was ultimately denied by the Court on May 20, 2026. The Court entered judgment in Defendant’s favor that same day.

Now before the Court is Plaintiff’s motion to set aside/vacate the May 20, 2026, judgment on the grounds that another action affecting the outcome of the proceedings before this Court is purportedly presently pending before the Compton, California branch of the Los Angeles Superior Court as 22CMCV00753, Smith v. Michael Kors Inc. (the “Santa Monica action”). (See Motion, p. 2, ¶ 4.)

The motion is DENIED, with prejudice.

Plaintiff’s motion is noticed as being premised on Code of Civil Procedure sections 473, subdivision (d), and 1008, subdivisions (a), (b), and (e). (Motion, pp. 1-2.) Both premises fail.

As argued in Defendant’s opposition, there is no applicable provision of Code of Civil Procedure section 473, subdivision (d), here. (See Opposition pp. 11-12.) Plaintiff is asking that the Court vacate a final judgment based on the purported pendency of the Santa Monica action. This is not a valid ground for relief under section 473, subdivision (d), which is limited to clerical errors and void judgments and orders, including those voided by extrinsic fraud or mistake, neither of which Plaintiff’s paper show. (See Kramer v. Traditional Escrow, Inc. (2020) 56 Cal.App.5th 13, 29 [discussing § 473, subd. (d)].)

Similarly, none of the grounds for party-requested reconsideration—new or different facts, circumstances, or law (Code Civ. Proc., § 1008, subd. (a))—appear here, as the requested relief is based on the purported pendency of the Santa Monica action rather than some fact, circumstance, or new law relating to this action.

Last, the Court takes judicial notice of Exhibit A attached to Defendant’s opposition, which shows a June 18, 2026, minute order for the Santa Monica action, in which the court in that case denied a similar motion by Plaintiff in this case to vacate or set aside the judgment in that case, which was entered on November 6, 2025. (Opposition, Request for Judicial Notice, Ex. A, pp. 6-7.)

Plaintiff’s motion is accordingly DENIED. No further motions seeking identical relief shall be entertained absent a proper statutory basis.

Plaintiff Michael B. Smith is ordered to give notice.

Parties who intend to submit on this tentative must send an email to the court at [email protected] indicating intention to submit on the tentative as directed by the instructions provided on the court website at www.lacourt.org. If the department does not receive an email indicating the parties are submitting on the tentative and there are no appearances at the hearing, the motion may be placed off calendar. If a party submits on the tentative, the party’s

email must include the case number and must identify the party submitting on the tentative. If the parties do not submit on the tentative, they should arrange to appear remotely.

Case Number: 21STCV26907    Hearing Date: July 30, 2026    Dept: 731

[TENTATIVE] ORDER RE: APPLICATION FOR PRO HAC VICE ADMISSION OF KENNETH J. PEACE TO APPEAR AS COUNSEL FOR DEFENDANT



  1. Background Facts

Plaintiff Ernest Melendrez sues various Defendants pursuant to an October 26, 2022, First Amended Complaint (“FAC”) alleging various statutory and common law claims arising from Plaintiff’s employment with Defendant, who alleges to have experienced disability discrimination and unlawful termination during that employment.

Now before the Court is a pro hac vice application for admission of Kenneth J. Peace, Esq., as counsel for Defendants, which Plaintiff Melendrez opposes.

  1. Application for Pro Hac Vice Admission

a.     Legal Standard

Out-of-state counsel may appear before a California court as counsel pro hac vice. (Birbrower, Montalbano, Condon & Frank v. Superior Court (1998) 17 Cal.4th 119, 130, as modified, Feb. 25, 1998.) To do so, out-of-state counsel must comply with requirements established in California Rules of Court, rule 9.40(a), (c), (d), and (e). (See Cal. Rules of Court, rule 9.40.)

A Pro Hac Vice application may be denied where: (1) the application fails to the follow the precepts of California Rules of Court, rule 9.40(c), (d) or (e); (2) the applicant is a California resident, regularly employed in California, or has other activities in California, (Cal. Rules of Court, rule 9.40(a)(1)-(a)(3)); or (3) absent special circumstances, the applicant has made repeated appearances under rule 9.40, (Cal. Rules of Court, rule 9.40(b)).

b.     Discussion

                              i.        Plaintiff’s Opposition Arguments

The Court initially notes that Plaintiff’s opposition arguments are no longer applicable or unavailing.

The opposition was filed as a declaration on the same day that the pro hac vice application was filed, i.e., June 1, 2026, on which date trial was set for June 15, 2026, a mere 14 days later. However, on June 5, 2026, the Court continued trial to July 13, 2026, and, pursuant to a July 13, 2026, stipulation by the parties at the final status conference, was further continued to October 23, 2026. Therefore, the arguments in the opposition relating to proximity of trial date supporting a denial of relief no longer apply.

As for Plaintiff’s other arguments—essentially that pro hac vice counsel is too often practicing law in California and current defense counsel is more than adequately staffed to handle this case—they are unavailing because the Court does not agree with the first position, as reflected by the facts in the Peace declaration, and the second point is irrelevant to whether relief should be granted.

                             ii.        Cal. Rules of Court, rule 9.40(a)

Moving to the merits, the pro hac vice application satisfies this rule of court, which requires that a pro hac vice application demonstrate that the applicant is:

(1)           A member in good standing of another state bar eligible to practice in any United State courts or the highest court in another jurisdiction (see Amended Application, Peace Decl., ¶ 6 [admission in four states]); and

(2)           Associated with an active member of the California Bar as attorney of record (id. at ¶ 10).

(Cal. Rules of Court, rule 9.40(a).)

                            iii.        Cal. Rules of Court, rule 9.40(c)

The pro hac vice application satisfies this rule of court, which requires that when a pro hac vice application is filed in a superior court, that application and its proof of service must satisfy the requirements set out in California Rules of Court, rule 9.40(c)(1), under which the applicant must:

(1) File with the court a verified application (see Amended Petition, Peace Decl., ¶ 1 & verification);

(2) File a proof of service showing service of the application and the notice of hearing on all parties who have appeared in the case and on the State Bar of California at its San Francisco office (see Amended Petition, Peace Decl., ¶ 11 & Proof of Service [service on other parties and on State Bar via portal]); and

(3) Provide notice of hearing in the time prescribed in Code of Civil Procedure section 1005 unless the court has prescribed a shorter period (see Amended Petition, Proof of Service).

(See Cal. Rules of Court, rule 9.40(c)(1).)

                            iv.        Cal. Rules of Court, rule 9.40(d)

The pro hac vice application satisfies this rule of court, which requires that a pro hac vice application provide:

(1) The applicant's residence and office address (Amended Petition, Peace Decl., ¶¶ 3, 4);

(2) The courts to which the applicant has been admitted to practice and the dates of admission (id. at ¶ 6);

(3) That the applicant is a licensee in good standing in those courts (id. at ¶ 7);

(4) That the applicant is not currently suspended or disbarred in any court (id. at ¶ 8);

(5) The title of each court and cause in which the applicant has filed an application to appear as counsel pro hac vice in this state in the preceding two years, the date of each application, and whether or not it was granted (id. at ¶ 9); and

(6) The name, address, and telephone number of the active licensee of the State Bar of California who is attorney of record (id. at ¶ 10).

(Cal. Rules of Court, rule 9.40(d)(1)-(d)(6).)

                             v.        Cal. Rules of Court, rule 9.40(e)

 The pro hac vice application satisfies this rule of court, which requires that a pro hac vice application show payment of the required fee set by the State. (Amended Petition, Peace Decl., ¶ 12.)

c.     Conclusion

Accordingly, Kenneth J. Peace’s application is GRANTED.

Defendants are ordered to give notice. 

 

Parties who intend to submit on this tentative must send an email to the court at [email protected] indicating intention to submit on the tentative as directed by the instructions provided on the court website at www.lacourt.org.  If the department does not receive an email indicating the parties are submitting on the tentative and there are no appearances at the hearing, the motion may be placed off calendar.  If a party submits on the tentative, the party’s email must include the case number and must identify the party submitting on the tentative.  If the parties do not submit on the tentative, they should arrange to appear remotely.

[TENTATIVE] ORDER RE: PLAINTIFF’S MOTION FOR SUMMARY ADJUDICATION [CRS # 4455] 

 

Dept. 731 

July 30, 2026 

8:30 A.M. 

Matter No. 17

[TENTATIVE] ORDER RE: DEFENDANT LAWRENCE J. SHUMAN’S MOTION FOR SUMMARY ADJUDICATION [CRS # 9477] 

 

Dept. 731 

July 30, 2026 

8:30 A.M. 

Matter No. 17 

Rebekah Shuman Motion for Summary Adjudication [CRS # 4455] 

Moving Party: Plaintiff, Rebekah Shuman 

Opposing Party: Defendant, Lawrence J. Shuman, individually and in his capacity as a co-trustee of The 2020 Shuman Family Trust 

Notice: OK 

Lawrence Shuman Motion for Summary Adjudication [CRS # 9477] 

Moving Party: Defendant, Lawrence J. Shuman, individually and in his capacity as a co-trustee of The 2020 Shuman Family Trust 

Opposing Party: Plaintiff, Rebekah Shuman 

Notice: OK 

 

  1. Background Facts 

Plaintiff Rebekah Shuman (“Plaintiff”) sues Defendant Lawrence J. Shuman (“Defendant”), individually and in his capacity as a co-trustee of The 2020 Shuman Family Trust, and Nominal Defendant The Shuman Management Company, Inc. (“TSMC”) pursuant to a March 1, 2023, Complaint alleging claims of (1) Breach of Express Contract, (2) Breach of Implied-In-Fact Contract, (3) Fraud, (4) Breach of Fiduciary Duty, (5) Breach of Fiduciary Duty, (6) Quiet Title, (7) Conversion, (8) Accounting, (9) Failure to Produce Corporate Books and Records, (10) Constructive Trust, and (11) Declaratory Relief. 

The claims arise from allegations that following a twenty-three year romantic relationship, including more than ten years of marriage, the parties in this action separated, since which time Defendant has attempted to shut out Plaintiff from receipt of her one-half interest in the assets acquired by the parties throughout their relationship, including but not limited to the couple’s successful literary and production company, TSMC, that was built together by both Defendant and Plaintiff during their twenty-three (23)-year romantic relationship and marriage. 

Now before the Court are: 

(1) Plaintiff’s opposed January 22, 2026, motion for summary adjudication of the Complaint’s first, third, fourth, and seventh causes of action for Breach of Contract, Fraud, Breach of Fiduciary Duty, and Conversion (CRS # 4455) (originally set for hearing on April 30, 2026; opposition filed by Defendant on April 15, 2026; reply filed by Plaintiff on April 24, 2026; hearing continued to June 18, 2026, on April 29, 2026, per parties’ stipulation; hearing continued to July 30, 2026, on June 18, 2026, as based on peremptory challenge to judicial officer); and 

(2) Defendant’s opposed March 27, 2026, motion for summary judgment or, in the alternative, summary adjudication of the Complaint’s eleven causes of action (CRS # 9477) (originally set for hearing on June 18, 2026; opposition filed by Plaintiff on May 29, 2026; reply filed by Defendant on June 5, 2026; hearing continued to July 30, 2026, on June 18, 2026, as based on peremptory challenge to judicial officer). 

 

  1. Plaintiff’s Motion for Summary Adjudication [CRS # 4455] 

  1. Evidentiary Objections 

NOT RULED ON: All objections (Code Civ. Proc., § 437c, subd. (q)) 

OVERRULED: None 

SUSTAINED: None 

  1. Discussion 

After review, the Court DENIES Plaintiff’s motion on procedural grounds. 

“Trial courts should not hesitate to deny summary judgment motions when the moving party fails to draft a compliant separate statement,” such as a “separate statement [that] includes an overly long document that includes multiple nonmaterial facts in violation of the Rules of Court.” (Beltran v. Hard Rock Hotel Licensing, Inc. (2023) 97 Cal.App.5th 865, 876 (Beltran).) 

First, Code of Civil Procedure section 437c, subdivision (b)(1), requires each motion for summary judgment to be accompanied by a separate statement “setting forth plainly and concisely all material facts that the moving party contends are undisputed.” In turn, California Rules of Court, rule 3.1350(d)(2) provides that the “separate statement should include only material facts and not any facts that are not pertinent to the disposition of the motion.” Under the Rules of Court, “‘[m]aterial facts’ are facts that relate to the cause of action, claim for damages, issue of duty, or affirmative defense that is the subject of the motion and that could make a difference in the disposition of the motion.” (Cal. Rules of Court, rule 3.1350(a)(2).) Courts may deny a summary judgment or adjudication motion failing to comply with this requirement. (See Beltran, supra, 97 Cal.App.5th at p. 876 [“an inappropriate separate statement includes an overly long document that includes multiple nonmaterial facts in violation of the Rules of Court”].) 

Here, the separate statement attached to the moving papers includes undisputed material facts comprised of multiple passages and supporting pieces of evidence, not all of which are material to the disposition of the issues at hand. For example, in UMF No. 5, the separate statement discusses the parties’ conception of two children and fertility efforts within the context of putatively seeking summary adjudication of the first cause of action for breach of express contract, thus showing non-material facts. 

Second and on a related point, the separate statement filed by Plaintiff combines multiple factual propositions in a single undisputed material fact and confusingly does not directly, 1:1 correspond the cited evidence to the cited factual propositions. (See, e.g., Motion, Separate Statement, UMF No. 7 [multiple sentence paragraph in left-hand column, without citations to evidence at the end of each sentence, and with the cited evidence presented in a separate column altogether].) This violates California Rule of Court, rules 3.1350(d)(3), providing that a separate statement must cite proposition of fact, directly followed by a prescribed citation to evidence, presented in a two-column format, as required by subsection (h). The separate statement also violates rule 3.1350(h), which sets the two-column format for a separate statement, with the moving party’s material facts and evidence stated in the left-hand column, and the opposing party’s material facts and evidence presented in a column on the right. Subsection (h) on its face provides various illustrations of proper formatting, which a comparison to Plaintiff’s separate statement shows were not followed. (Compare Cal. Rules of Court, rule 3.1350(h) [In an example of proper formatting, in the left column, stating: “Plaintiff and defendant entered into a written contract for the sale of widgets. Jackson declaration, 2:17-21; contract, Ex. A to Jackson declaration.”], with, e.g., Motion, Separate Statement, UMF No. 7 [multiple sentence paragraph in left-hand column, without citations to evidence at the end of each sentence, and with the cited evidence presented in a separate column altogether].) This deficiency contrasts with the separate statement filed by Plaintiff in opposition to a separate motion for adjudication by Defendant, which more closely follows these rules of court. (See May 20, 2026, Separate Statement [CRS # 9477].)  

Third, Plaintiff’s papers violate California Rules of Court, rule 3.1350(b), which requires that (1) a motion summary adjudication specifically state in the notice of motion the specific cause of action, affirmative defense, claims for damages, or issues of duty on which summary adjudication is sought, and (2) the foregoing statements in the notice be repeated verbatim in the separate statement. 

Here, the 3.1350(b) statements in Plaintiff’s notice of motion do not verbatim match her separate statement. (Compare, e.g., Motion, 2:16-20 [notice of motion re: third and fourth causes of action], with Motion, Separate Statement, § 3 at p. 17 [corresponding header in separate statement not copied over verbatim].) This omission—beyond being a violation of the rule itself and thus a basis for denial (see Beltran, supra, 97 Cal.App.5th at p. 876)—lent great confusion to the papers. For example, Plaintiff’s notice of motion seeks summary adjudication of the first cause of action for breach of express contract, but the points and authorities instead focus on seeking summary adjudication of the second cause of action for breach of implied-in-fact contract. (Compare Complaint, ¶¶ 65-90, with id. at ¶¶ 91-101 [express and implied breach of contract claims]; also compare Motion, 2:12-15 [notice attacking first cause of action], with id. at pp. 6-20 [presential arguments for implied-in-fact breach of contract].) 

The Court may deny summary adjudication under the above circumstances. (Beltran, supra, 97 Cal.App.5th at p. 876.) 

  1. Conclusion 

Plaintiff Rebekah Shuman’s Motion for Summary Adjudication [CRS # 4455] is accordingly DENIED. 

 

  1. Defendant’s Motion for Summary Adjudication [CRS # 9477] 

  1. Evidentiary Objections 

NOT RULED ON: All objections (Code Civ. Proc., § 437c, subd. (q)) 

SUSTAINED: None 

OVERRULED: None 

  1. Legal Standard 

A motion for summary judgment shall be granted if all the papers submitted show that there is no triable issue as to any material fact for trial or that the moving party is entitled to a judgment as a matter of law. (Code of Civ. Proc., § 437c, subd. (c).) A party may also seek summary adjudication of select causes of action, affirmative defenses, claims for damages, or issues of duty, which may be made by a standalone motion or as an alternative to a motion for summary judgment and proceeds in all procedural respects like a motion for summary judgment, but which must completely dispose of the challenged cause of action, affirmative defense, claim for damages, or issue of duty. (Code Civ. Proc., § 437c, subds. (f)(1)-(2), (t).) 

The moving party bears the initial burden of production to make prima facie showing no triable material fact issues. (Aguilar v. Atlantic Richfield Co. (2001) 25 Cal.4th 826, 850.) This burden on summary judgment or adjudication “is more properly one of persuasion rather than proof, since he must persuade the court that there is no material fact for a reasonable trier of fact to find, and not to prove any such fact to the satisfaction of the court itself as though it were sitting as the trier of fact.” (Id. at p. 850, fn. 11.) If the moving party meets this burden, the burden shifts to the opposing party to make a rebuttal prima facie showing that a triable issue of material fact exists. (Id. at p. 849.) 

Where a defendant seeks summary judgment or adjudication, the defendant must show that either “one or more elements of the cause of action, even if not separately pleaded, cannot be established, or that there is a complete defense to that cause of action.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 437c, subd. (o)(2).) A defendant may satisfy this burden by showing that the claim “cannot be established” because of the lack of evidence on some essential element of the claim. (Union Bank v. Superior Court (1995) 31 Cal.App.4th 574, 590.) Once the defendant meets this burden, the burden shifts to the plaintiff to show that a “triable issue of one or more material facts exists as to that cause of action or defense thereto.” (Ibid.)  “[I]n ruling on motions for summary judgment courts are to ‘“liberally construe the evidence in support of the party opposing summary judgment and resolve doubts concerning the evidence in favor of that party.”‘ [Citations].” (Cheal v. El Camino Hospital (2014) 223 Cal.App.4th 736, 760.). 

  1. Discussion 

  1. Summary Adjudication, First Cause of Action 

Plaintiff’s first cause of action alleges a breach of an express contract (a “Grand Promise” allegedly made by Defendant verbally to Plaintiff in 1999) based on Defendant filing for divorce on August 22, 2022, which, based on the terms sought by Defendant in the divorce, breached the promises in the Grand Promise to divide assets for Plaintiff’s benefit and provide her with continued financial support for the rest of her life. (Complaint, ¶¶ 65-90 [entire cause of action, with above facts at ¶ 87].) 

In his motion, Defendant argues that the first cause of action fails on summary adjudication because (1) it is beyond its statute of limitations and (2) remediative theories for a lapse in the limitations period, e.g., the discovery rule or fraud, among others, are inapplicable. (Motion, pp. 10-14.) 

After review, the Court determines that Defendant fails to carry his burden on summary adjudication. 

A breach of contract claim based on a contract not in writing is subject to a two-year statute of limitations. (Code Civ. Proc., § 339.) A statute of limitations starts to run once the cause of action “accrues,” and although a cause of action typically accrues when it is complete with all of its elements, a cause of action will at times be deemed to accrue at a later date, such as when the plaintiff did not discover and had no occasion to discover the cause of action until that later date (the discovery rule), when the defendant fraudulently concealed the existence of a possible claim until that later date, or when the defendant committed multiple wrongs that ended on that later date (the continuing violations doctrine). (Doe v. Roman Catholic Archbishop of Los Angeles (2016) 247 Cal.App.4th 953, 961.) 

Here, the Complaint alleges that “[y]ear after year, Rebekah and Larry continually reaffirmed and ratified their agreement(s), including without limitation, Larry’s ‘Grand Promise’” (Complaint, ¶ 78), and that the Grand Promise was breached on August 22, 2022, when Defendant filed for divorce. (Complaint, ¶ 76.) 

These theories for liability must be addressed in the moving papers because a defendant moving for summary judgment has the burden “to identify and respond to all theories of liability reflected in the complaint, ‘even if not separately pleaded.’ [Citation.] … While a plaintiff … need sustain its burden of proof only on one of the theories in order to prevail at trial, a defendant who seeks a summary judgment must define all of the theories alleged in the complaint and challenge each factually.’” (Lopez v. Superior Court (1996) 45 Cal.App.4th 705, 714 (Lopez); see Johnson v. Chui (2011) 199 Cal.App.4th 775, 778 [“[A] defendant is entitled to summary judgment only when all theories of liability have been negated”]; Farley v. El Tejon Unified School Dist. (1990) 225 Cal.App.3d 371, 379 [“[T]o prevail on its motion for summary judgment, [the defendant] had the burden of negating every alternative theory of liability presented by the pleadings”].) Where a motion for summary judgment does “‘not negate theories of [the defendant’s] liability, the trial court should’” rule “‘[the defendant] failed to carry [its] initial burden and stop[] there.’” (Hedayati v. Interinsurance Exchange of the Automobile Club (2021) 67 Cal.App.5th 833, 846; see Hawkins v. Wilton (2006) 144 Cal.App.4th 936, 945.)  

Here, while the moving papers argue that a number of remediating theories for breach of contract do not apply (including the discovery rule), there is no evidence before the Court to negate the allegation in the Complaint that “[y]ear after year, Rebekah and Larry continually reaffirmed and ratified their agreement(s),” with Defendant allegedly only breaching the Grand Promise on August 22, 2022. (Complaint, ¶¶ 76, 78.) Instead, Defendant points to numerous acts by Defendants over the years that putatively should have put Plaintiff on notice that the Grand Promise had been breached well before August 22, 2022. (Motion, pp. 10-14.) However, such arguments do not address the allegation that the Grand Promise was reaffirmed and ratified year after year between 1999 and 2022. Consequently, Defendant presents evidence on the one hand to show Plaintiff was on notice of breach well before August 2022, while on the other hand failing to negate the theory that Defendant reaffirmed and ratified the Grand Promise from year to year. Even if the Court accepted Defendant’s arguments and evidence, this inconsistency alone shows triable issues of material fact as to the first cause of action for failure to capture and negate all of Plaintiff’s theories in support of the claim. 

Summarized, for failure to negate the “year after year” allegation, Defendant has failed to show that no triable issues of material fact remain as to whether breach occurred before expiration of the statute of limitations, where the Complaint alleges a breach date of August 22, 2022, and this action was filed less than a year later on March 1, 2023. 

Defendant’s motion for summary adjudication of the first cause of action is thus DENIED. 

  1. Summary Adjudication, Second Cause of Action 

The Complaint’s second cause of action alleges that through implied conduct, Defendant separately entered into a contract with Plaintiff whereby at Defendant’s request, Plaintiff gave up various goals and career opportunities which would have benefitted her in the future so that she would be able to devote most of her time and attention to Defendant’s personal needs as called upon, with the continued assurance that she would then and in the future, in case of the termination of their relationship, obtain a division of the parties’ assets and that she would be rendered financially secure. (Complaint, ¶¶ 91-101 [above proposition at ¶ 96.a.].) 

As with the first cause of action, Defendant argues on summary adjudication that the second cause of action is beyond its statute of limitations and not subject to remediating theories. (Motion, pp. 14-15.) 

However, a review of the second cause of action shows that it is subject to the same reasoning as the first cause of action vis-à-vis the statute of limitations. Specifically, the Complaint alleges that “[y]ear after year, Rebekah and Larry continually reaffirmed and ratified their agreement(s), including without limitation, Larry’s ‘Grand Promise’” (Complaint, ¶ 78), with Defendant thereafter breaching the parties’ implied-in-fact agreements on August 22, 2022, when he filed for divorce and repudiated his obligations under the implied-in-fact agreements. (Complaint, ¶¶ 91 [incorporating prior allegations, including ¶ 78], 97 [breach of implied agreements on August 22, 2022, at initiation of divorce proceedings].) 

Consequently, on the same reasoning as discussed in relation to the first cause of action, the Court determines that Defendant fails to carry his burden to show that no triable issues of material fact remain as to whether breach occurred before expiration of the statute of limitations, where the Complaint alleges a breach date of August 22, 2022, and this action was filed less than a year later on March 1, 2023. 

Accordingly, Defendant’s motion for summary adjudication is DENIED as to the second cause of action. 

  1. Summary Adjudication, Third Cause of Action 

The Complaint’s third cause of action alleges fraud against Defendant based on two distinct misrepresentations: (1) the Grand Promise made in 1999 regarding care and assets, which Defendant never intended to honor when the Promise was made; and (2) a 2001 misrepresentation by Defendant at the time it was made, to the effect that Defendant would not hold against Plaintiff quitclaim deeds conveying Plaintiff’s interest in certain real property to Defendant (the Las Casas property), used to obtain more favorable terms on purchase of a separate property (the Albright property), with Defendant promising to hold Plaintiff’s conveyed 50% interest in the Las Casas property in trust for Plaintiff. (Complaint, ¶¶ 103-108.) 

The Complaint also points to Defendant’s receipt of sale proceeds of the Albright property in 2014 as supporting the fraud claim, which the Court reads as exposition of how Plaintiff continued to rely on the 2001 promise relating to the Las Casas and Albright properties rather than as a misrepresentation in and of itself, particularly where a deposit of funds is not a misrepresentation as contemplated in fraud claims. (Complaint, ¶ 108 [“By [his] acceptance of the funds from the sale of the Albright Street Property, [Defendant] continued to perpetrate a fraud upon [Plaintiff] and induce her into believing all assets acquired by the Parties were joint assets that were equally owned, regardless of the manner of which title was held.”].) 

Defendant challenges this claim on summary adjudication, arguing that the 1999 Grand Promise and 2001 representations, if fraudulent, ran their statute of limitations well before this action was filed, with the Grand Promise running its limitations period by January 2004 (three years after the representation is alleged to have been made), and the 2001 representation running its limitations period by July 2004 (three years after the representation is alleged to have been made). (Motion, pp. 16-17). 

After review, the Court determines that Defendant fails to carry his burden on summary adjudication. 

“An action for relief on the ground of fraud” is subject to a three-year statute of limitations, where “[t]he cause of action in that case is not deemed to have accrued until the discovery, by the aggrieved party, of the facts constituting the fraud ….” (Code Civ. Proc., § 338, subd. (d).) 

Here, the Complaint provides sufficient allegations to set an alleged discovery date of August 22, 2022, when the divorce proceedings were initiated. (Complaint, ¶¶ 78, 102, 110.) 

In his motion for summary adjudication, Defendant argues that the limitations periods here began from the date on which the representations were made, citing Fox v. Ethicon Endo-Surgery, Inc. (2005) 35 Cal.4th 797, 807 in support. (Motion, pp. 16-17.) 

However, the plain face of section 338, subdivision (d) is clear: “An action for relief on the ground of fraud” is subject to a three-year statute of limitations, where “[t]he cause of action in that case is not deemed to have accrued until the discovery, by the aggrieved party, of the facts constituting the fraud ….”  

Critically, Defendant’s citation to Fox is misplaced. Fox discusses the law behind accrual for a cause of action, where, at most, the court stated that a cause of action begins to accrue when the plaintiff has suspicion of one element of a claim coupled with knowledge of the other elements of that claim, and that lack of knowledge as to a defendant’s identity in that case did not impede the limitations period from running because the defendant’s identity was not an element of the cause of action. (Fox, supra, at p. 807.) Defendant is admonished for citing a published authority to support a proposition for which the cited authority does not stand. 

Accordingly, summary adjudication of the Complaint’s third cause of action DENIED. 

  1. Summary Adjudication, Fourth Cause of Action 

The fourth cause of action alleges a breach of fiduciary duty from Defendant to Plaintiff based on Plaintiff’s 2001 quitclaim deed, and based on Defendant’s corresponding representations to not hold the quitclaim deeds against Plaintiff, which created a fiduciary duty to Plaintiff with respect to the interest Defendant should have been holding in trust for Plaintiff, and which Defendant breached when he filed for divorce on August 22, 2022, alleging that the Las Casas property was his sole and separate property, thus depriving Plaintiff of her interest in that property. (Complaint, ¶¶ 113-117.) 

Defendant challenges the fourth cause of action on summary adjudication on the grounds that no triable issues exist as to (1) a duty from Defendant to Plaintiff or (2) whether the limitations period has run on the claim. (Motion, pp. 18-19.) 

The Court addresses each ground in turn. 

  1. Duty 

In support of the ‘no duty exist’ argument on summary adjudication, Defendant argues that Maglica v. Maglica (1998) 66 Cal.App.4th 442 purportedly holds that, without entrustment of property, or an oral agreement to purchase property together, there can be no fiduciary relationship no matter how ‘confidential’ a relationship between an unmarried, cohabiting couple. (Motion, p. 18.) 

While this proposition of law is correct insofar as it goes, it does not carry Defendant’s burden on summary adjudication. 

The Complaint in fact alleges that Plaintiff’s interest in the Las Casas property would be held by Defendant in trust for her, and that Defendant acted against his promise to hold Plaintiff’s interest in trust when he initiated divorce proceedings and claimed Plaintiff had no interest in the property. (Complaint, ¶¶ 114-116.) 

In his motion, as against the 2001 representations, Defendant argues the quitclaim deeds executed by Plaintiff in 2001 on their face negate any entrustment theory because in effect they do not retain for Plaintiff any interest in the property. (See Motion, 18:18-25.) 

However, nowhere do the moving papers address, in relation to the fourth cause of action, why Defendant’s alleged promise to hold a 50% interest in the Las Casas property in spite of Plaintiff’s execution of the quitclaim deeds—a theory explicitly alleged in the Complaint (see, e.g., Complaint, ¶ 114)—constitutes entrustment for duty purposes. 

Consequently, the moving papers do not negate all theories for liability alleged in the Complaint in relation to the fourth cause of action, for which reason summary adjudication against the fourth cause of action cannot be granted on the ground that no triable issues exist as to duty. (Lopez, supra, 45 Cal.App.4th at p. 714.) 

  1. Statute of Limitations 

Defendant next contends that the statute of limitations period ran on the breach of fiduciary claim four years after the alleged 2001 representations. (Motion, pp. 18-19.) 

The Court finds this position unavailing. 

Ante, with respect to the third cause of action, the Court determined that triable issues remain as to when the limitations period was triggered in relation to duties arising from the 2001 agreement, reasoning that triable issues remained as to whether the 2001 promises were breached on the alleged date of August 22, 2022. 

Because the fourth cause of action—subject to a four-year limitations period (Code Civ. Proc., § 343 [catch-all provision])—arises from the transactions involved in the third cause of action, i.e., the 2001 transactions, the Court adopts like reasoning to determine that triable issues remain as to whether discovery of the harm contemplated in the fourth cause of action occurred before August 22, 2022, as alleged in the Complaint, undercutting Defendant’s limitations position here. 

Having failed to carry his burden on either theory for summary adjudication of the fourth cause of action, such relief is DENIED.  

  1. Summary Adjudication, Fifth Cause of Action 

The Complaint’s fifth cause of action alleges breach of fiduciary duties owed to Plaintiff by Defendant, to wit, breach of duties owed by Defendant as shareholder, member, and officer in Defendant TSMC, arising from Defendant’s failure to account for Plaintiff’s interest in the company, use of TSMC monies to pay personal obligations, refusal to pay owed income to Plaintiff, and wrongfully asserting Plaintiff has no interest in TSMC. (Complaint, ¶¶ 121-125.d.) 

Defendant moves for summary adjudication of this cause of action on two grounds: (1) Plaintiff never acquired an interest in TSMC, where Plaintiff’s only two pieces of evidence to show such an interest—a non-endorsed stock certificate, and listing of Plaintiff on K-1 schedules filed by TSMC—fail to show transfer of an interest in TSMC to Plaintiff; and (2) the limitations period has run on this claim. (Motion, pp. 19-21.) 

After review, the Court determines that Defendant fails to carry his burden on both issues. 

Regarding interest in TSMC, the first and second causes of action survived summary adjudication, thus leaving triable issues as to whether, by way of express or implied agreements, Plaintiff acquired an interest in TSMC. (See, e.g., Complaint, ¶ 97 [In second cause of action, alleging that “[o]n or about August 22, 2022, [Defendant] took a position with regard to the Parties’ ownership of assets that was in direct contradiction to their long-standing agreement that all assets were owned equally by the Parties,” emphasis added].) Yet, Defendant’s argument is narrower, relating to whether an interest was gained in TSMC by Plaintiff through a stock certificate or representations in K-1 filings (Motion, pp. 19-21), as opposed to through implied conduct throughout the entirety of the parties’ relationship or equitable grounds. Because the latter ground presents triable issues as to whether Plaintiff acquired an interest in TSMC through implied conduct or equitable grounds, Defendant’s arguments do not negate all theories for showing that Plaintiff did in fact have an interest in TSMC. The motion, as based on this argument, must thus necessarily fail vis-à-vis the fifth cause of action. (Lopez, supra, 45 Cal.App.4th at p. 714.) 

As for the statute of limitations, without great elaboration or even providing a final limitations date, Defendant argues that breaches of the four duties alleged in the fifth cause of action were open and notorious long before this action was filed, triggering the limitations period, which elapsed long before this action was filed. (Motion, 21:14-24.) This argument is insufficiently elaborated to support relief here. (See (Motion, 21:14-24.) 

Accordingly, Defendant’s motion for summary adjudication is DENIED as to the fifth cause of action. 

  1. Summary Adjudication, Sixth Cause of Action 

The sixth cause of action alleges a quiet title claim seeking to confirm Plaintiff’s alleged 50% interest in the Las Casas property. (See Complaint, ¶¶ 130-136.) 

Defendant argues that the claim fails on summary adjudication because (1) laches forecloses relief to Plaintiff insofar as Plaintiff sat on her hands for more than 20 years between the 2001 transactions conveying Plaintiff’s interest in the subject property and the time this action was filed in 2023 and (2) because the underlying fraud claim failed, for which reason this derivative claim must also fail. (Motion, pp. 21-23.) 

After review, the Court determines Defendant failed to carry his burden on summary adjudication. 

As for laches, the argument is unavailing. In order to establish laches, the party must show: “(1) delay in asserting a right or a claim; (2) the delay was not reasonable or excusable; and (3) prejudice to the party against whom laches is asserted. [Citations.]” (Magic Kitchen LLC v. Good Things Internat., Ltd. (2007) 153 Cal.App.4th 1144, 1157 (Magic Kitchen).) Here, the Court adopts its discussion ante vis-à-vis the third and fourth causes of action to determine that because triable issues remain as to when the limitations period began to run on the 2001 transactions, triable issues remain as to whether laches (which requires unreasonable or inexcusable delay) forecloses relief on the sixth cause of action. 

As for the argument that this claim fails as derivative of the fraud claim, the fraud claim was not defeated on summary adjudication, undercutting this position. 

Summary adjudication of the sixth cause of action is accordingly DENIED. 

  1. Summary Adjudication, Seventh Cause of Action 

The Complaint’s seventh cause of action alleges conversion against Defendant arising from allegations that Defendants converted monies to which Plaintiff was entitled as part of their business partnership going back to 1999, ownership interests in mutually purchased real property, and a number of personal property items such as computers, appliances, and antiques. (Complaint, ¶¶ 137-142.) 

On summary adjudication, Defendant argues that the seventh cause of action only alleges conversion in two ways—wage conversion, and ERISA (retirement income) distribution conversion—and that any conversion by wage theft fails for various reasons. (Motion, pp. 23-24.) However, Defendant also explicitly declined to submit arguments as against ERISA conversion. (Motion, 23:27-24-4.) Moreover, Defendant’s motion fails to address the conversion of chattels alleged in the Complaint. (Complaint, ¶¶ 138-138.xiii.) Consequently, not all theories of liability for conversion alleged in the Complaint have been negated, for which summary adjudication as to the entire seventh cause of action (as sought here) must fail. (Lopez, supra, 45 Cal.App.4th at p. 714.) 

Accordingly, Defendant’s motion for summary adjudication is DENIED as to the seventh cause of action. 

  1. Summary Adjudication, Eighth Cause of Action 

The Complaint’s eighth cause of action alleges accounting against Defendants based on allegations that Plaintiff is a shareholder in TSMC and is thus entitled to an accounting with respect to outstanding distributions, dividends, and/or interest income, implicitly relying on pleading by incorporation to establish Plaintiff’s interest in TSMC. (See Complaint, ¶¶ 143, 144, 146.) 

On summary adjudication Defendant argues that the eighth cause of action fails because (1) the underlying first through fifth causes of action failed, (2) information asymmetry (equal accounting information held by Plaintiff, specifically through discovery in this action) exists here and defeats the accounting claim, and (3) Plaintiff lacks shareholder standing in TSMC. 

After review, the Court finds all three grounds unavailing on summary adjudication. 

First, summary adjudication of the first through fifth causes of action was denied. 

Second, Defendant insufficiently elaborated the grounds to support the position that information asymmetry forecloses relief here. (See Motion, 24:25-28.) A review of Defendant’s papers fails to show a pin cite for the cited authority, Sass v. Cohen (2020) 10 Cal.5th 861 (Sass). (See Motion, 24:25-28.) At most, and in relevant part, Sass appears to be cited for the proposition that “the underpinning of an accounting action is an information asymmetry between the parties, an asymmetry that generally favors the defendant but never the plaintiff.” (Sass, supra, at pp. 869-870.) However, citing such authority does nothing to carry Defendant’s burden to show how the facts before the Court show no triable issues as to the existence of information symmetry defeating the accounting claim. Defendant merely cites to discovery served by Plaintiff after this action was initiated to seemingly argue that because information symmetry occurred during discovery, Plaintiff’s accounting claim has been rendered moot. The Court rejects that position for lack of meaningful elaboration. 

Third, as discussed in relation to the fifth cause of action, triable issues remain as to whether Plaintiff is a shareholder of TSMC, which would entitle her to an accounting. 

Summary adjudication of the Complaint’s eighth cause of action is thus DENIED. 

  1. Summary Adjudication, Ninth Cause of Action 

The Complaint’s ninth cause of action alleges a claim of failure to produce corporate books and records against Defendants based on Defendants’ refusal to turn over these materials following Plaintiff’s February 23, 2023, demand for the same. (Complaint, ¶¶ 152-158.) 

Defendant here challenges the claim on summary adjudication, arguing that the claim fails here because (1) Plaintiff is not a shareholder in TSMC, (2) the pre-suit demand served six days before suit was filed fails to comply with the good faith requirement in the statute vis-à-vis demands, and (3) the lack of a valid stock certificate in favor of Plaintiff forecloses relief. 

After review, the Court determines all three arguments are unavailing. 

First, as discussed in relation to the fifth cause of action, triable issues remain as to whether Plaintiff is a shareholder of TSMC, which would entitle her to the records sought by way of this claim. 

Second, Defendant’s argument that a demand served six days before a suit is filed cannot amount to good faith is insufficiently elaborated for the Court to give credence to this position as applied to the facts before the Court. (Motion, 25:20-25.) 

Third, as discussed in relation to the fifth cause of action, even if stock were not issued, Defendant’s motion does not sufficiently address implied-in-fact or equitable grounds for Plaintiff having a 50% interest in TSMC, undermining Defendant’s last argument in support of summary adjudication of the ninth cause of action. 

Summary adjudication of the ninth cause of action is accordingly DENIED. 

  1. Summary Adjudication, Tenth Cause of Action 

The Court GRANTS summary adjudication of the tenth cause of action. 

As recognized by Defendant’s motion, a claim for ‘constructive trust’ is not a cognizable cause of action in California, but rather, is a form of remedy. (Glue-Fold, Inc. v. Slautterback Corp. (2000) 82 Cal.App.4th 1018, 1022-1023, fn. 3 [“… a … cause of action seeking imposition of a constructive trust” “is not an independent cause of action but merely a type of remedy for some categories of underlying wrong”].) 

While Defendant’s motion seeks to nevertheless resolve the issue of constructive trust, no such relief can be granted. The issue of constructive trust was raised within the context of challenging the tenth cause of action, which is not a viable cause of action, thus mooting further discussion on the topic. 

  1. Summary Adjudication, Eleventh Cause of Action 

The Complaint’s eleventh cause of action seeks a declaration of respective rights, duties, and obligations in TSMC. (Complaint, ¶ 165.) 

Defendant moves for summary adjudication of the declaratory relief claim on the grounds that (1) no justiciable controversy exists here where all underlying claims (causes of action 1 through 10) will have failed on summary adjudication and (2) this claim being derivative of the first ten causes of action, declaratory relief would need to be barred where its underlying claims are also barred by their statute of limitations. (Motion, pp. 26-27.) 

Both arguments fail. 

First, the Court has denied Defendant’s motion as to the first nine causes of action, including on the grounds that triable issues remain as to whether Plaintiff is a shareholder of TSMC. (See discussion for Fifth Cause of Action ante.) If triable issues remain as to that shareholder status, then triable issues remain as to respective rights, duties, and obligations in TSMC, as sought in this claim. 

Second, as discussed above, Defendant failed to carry his burden on his statute of limitation arguments, undermining his second position against the eleventh cause of action. 

Summary adjudication of the eleventh cause of action is accordingly DENIED. 

  1. Conclusion 

Defendant Lawrence J. Shuman’s Motion for Summary Adjudication [CRS # 9477] is: 

  1. GRANTED as to the tenth cause of action alleged in Plaintiff’s Complaint; and 

  1. DENIED as to the remaining causes of action alleged in Plaintiff’s Complaint. 

 

Defendant Lawrence J. Shuman is ordered to give notice.

DATED: July 30, 2026 _____________________________________ 

MARK C. KIM  

Judge of the Superior Court 

Case Number: 23STCV14105    Hearing Date: July 30, 2026    Dept: 731

[TENTATIVE] ORDER RE: PLAINTIFF’S MOTION FOR AWARD OF ATTORNEYS’ FEES

  1. Background Facts

Plaintiff CalPortland brought this action pursuant to a June 20, 2023, Complaint alleging various breach of contract and common count claims related to work performed by CalPortland on behalf of Defendants J&F Builders, Inc., as guaranteed in writing by Defendant Francisco Ramirez and Does 11 through 20.

The action resolved by way of affirmative summary judgment in favor of Plaintiff, with judgment entered on January 30, 2026.

Now before the Court is Plaintiff’s opposed motion for attorneys’ fees and costs, as based on a contract between the parties. The Court also sua sponte addresses the May 14, 2026, memorandum of costs filed and served by Plaintiff.

 

  1. Motion for Attorneys’ Fees and Costs

a.     Legal Standard

A prevailing party is entitled to recover costs as a matter of right. (Code Civ. Proc., § 1032, subds. (a)(4), (b).) Attorneys’ fees are also recoverable as costs when authorized by contract, statute, or law. (Code Civ. Proc., § 1033.5, subd. (a)(10).) Fees and costs are recoverable where a party rejects an offer made pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure section 998 offer and later fails to obtain a more favorable judgment or award.

The Court begins this inquiry “with the ‘lodestar,’ i.e., the number of hours reasonably expended multiplied by the reasonable hourly rate.” (PLCM Group v. Drexler (2000) 22 Cal.4th 1084, 1095 (PLCM Group).) From there, the “lodestar figure may then be adjusted [according to a multiplier enhancement] based on consideration of factors specific to the case, in order to fix the fee at the fair market value for the legal services provided.” (Ibid.) Relevant multiplier factors include “(1) the novelty and difficulty of the questions involved, (2) the skill displayed in presenting them, (3) the extent to which the nature of the litigation precluded other employment by the attorneys, [and] (4) the contingent nature of the fee award.” (Ketchum v. Moses (2001) 24 Cal.4th 1122, 1132.)

b.     Discussion

Plaintiff brings this motion seeking $39,390.50 in attorney’s fees in connection with this action, as based on a contract between the parties, which is not attached to the moving papers, but which Defendant does not dispute in its opposition, limiting arguments to the reasonability of the award sought.

                              i.        Reasonable Rates

As to fee rates, Plaintiff seeks hourly rates ranging from $380.00 to $430.00 for counsel, and $175.00 to $210.00 for counsel’s paralegal. (See Motion, Lipschultz Decl., ¶¶ 7, 8, Exs. A, B.)

In opposition, Defendant argues that the rates are not properly supported by evidence addressing the prevailing rate for related work in the community. (Opposition, p. 5.)

The reply does not appreciably respond to the opposition.

After review, the Court finds that both counsel’s and counsel’s paralegal’s rates are reasonable. Critically, the Court is considered “an expert in the matter of attorney fees” insofar “[t]he value of attorney’s services is a matter with which a judge must necessarily be familiar.” (Excelsior Union High Sch. Dist. of L.A. Cnty. v. Lautrup (1969) 269 Cal.App.2d 434, 448.) Accordingly, “[w]hen the court is informed of the extent and nature of such services, its own experience furnishes it with every element necessary to fix their value.” (Ibid.)

Here, the Court’s own experience furnishes It with the background to confirm that the rates sought by Plaintiff for counsel and staff are eminently reasonable. Ms. Lipschultz is a 40-year practitioner (Motion, Lipschultz Decl., ¶ 10) whose skills were demonstrated by the record before the Court, including the successful affirmative motion for summary judgment leading to judgment here. As for staff, billings of $210.00 per hour for similar work in the community are not uncommon, supporting the requested rate.

                             ii.        Reasonable Hours

The number of hours spent on this action by counsel are not elaborated in the moving papers, not readily stated in or calculable from the attachments to the moving papers, and not clarified in the reply.

In opposition, Defendant argues that at least 13.8 hours of attorney time should be reduced from the total based on (1) 3.4 hours arising from bankruptcy proceedings related to a different defendant (Defendant Ramirez), against whom Plaintiff’s motion seeks no fees (see Motion, 2:5-7), and (2) 10.4 hours arising from invoices connected to a different if related action concerning the same construction project. Defendant also argues that Plaintiff’s remaining entries are rendered vague by block billing, meriting a 20% reduction in fees.

The reply does not appreciably respond to Defendant’s opposition arguments.

The Court agrees that the 17.2 hours of attorney time highlighted by Defendant are not recoverable by Plaintiff, but the Court declines to further reduce the hours expended on this action, which are shown to be reasonable by a juxtaposition of the tasks described in Plaintiff’s time entries and the corresponding time expended thereon, such as the number of hours reasonably expended on the summary judgment motion that led to judgment in this action.

Fees are thus reasonable in the amount of $32,337.30, calculated by subtracting the $7,053.20 in fees suggested by Defendant (Opposition, 4:10-15) from the total fees request of $39,390.50.

                            iii.        Multiplier

No multiplier is requested by the moving papers despite the papers’ discussion of the four multiplier factors, for which reason the Court does not further discuss this topic.

c.     Conclusion

Plaintiff’s motion is GRANTED in the amount of $32,337.30.

  1. Memorandum of Costs

a.     Legal Standard

A prevailing party who claims costs must serve and file a memorandum of costs within 15 days after the date of service of the notice of entry of judgment or dismissal by the clerk under Code of Civil Procedure section 664.5 or the date of service of written notice of entry of judgment or dismissal, or within 180 days after entry of judgment, whichever is first. (Cal. Rules of Court, rule 3.1700(a)(1).)

b.     Discussion

Though not directly before the Court, the Court addresses the May 14, 2026, memorandum of costs filed by Plaintiff.

After review, the Court determines that costs were untimely petitioned.

Judgment was entered on January 30, 2026, notice of judgment was served and filed by Plaintiff on February 26, 2026, and Plaintiff’s memorandum of costs was filed on May 14, 2026. Thus, because the notice of entry of judgment was served on February 26, 2026, the memorandum of costs was due 15 days from February 26, 2026, well before Plaintiff filed the memorandum of costs on May 14, 2026.

c.     Conclusion

Plaintiff’s request for costs pursuant to its May 14, 2026, memorandum of costs is thus DENIED.

Plaintiff is ordered to give notice. 

 

Parties who intend to submit on this tentative must send an email to the court at [email protected] indicating intention to submit on the tentative as directed by the instructions provided on the court website at www.lacourt.org.  If the department does not receive an email indicating the parties are submitting on the tentative and there are no appearances at the hearing, the motion may be placed off calendar.  If a party submits on the tentative, the party’s email must include the case number and must identify the party submitting on the tentative.  If the parties do not submit on the tentative, they should arrange to appear remotely.

SUPERIOR COURT OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA

GENERAL MOTORS LLC, a Delaware Limited Liability Company; and DOES 1 through 10, inclusive,

[TENTATIVE] ORDER RE: PLAINTIFF’S MOTION TO TAX COSTS

 

Dept. 731

July 30, 2026

8:30 A.M.

Matter No. 16

 

Moving Party:               Plaintiff, Melody Vivian McCullough

Opposing Party:           Defendant, General Motors LLC

Notice:                         OK

 

  1. Background Facts

Plaintiff Melody Vivian McCullough (“Plaintiff”) brought this lemon law action against Defendant General Motors LLC (“Defendant”) alleging various breaches of statutory law.

Judgment was entered in this action on October 30, 2025, in light of this Court’s grant of summary judgment in favor of Defendant. The clerk of the court gave notice of judgment to the parties one day later, on October 31, 2025.

Now before the Court is Plaintiff’s opposed May 12, 2026, motion to tax the memorandum of costs filed by Defendant on April 23, 2026.

 

  1. Motion to Strike or Tax Costs

a.     Legal Standard

A prevailing party who claims costs must serve and file a memorandum of costs [1] within 15 days after [a] the date of service of the notice of entry of judgment or dismissal by the clerk under Code of Civil Procedure section 664.5 or [b] the date of service of written notice of entry of judgment or dismissal, or [2] within 180 days after entry of judgment, whichever is first. (Cal. Rules of Court, rule 3.1700(a)(1), brackets added.) The memorandum of costs must be verified by a statement of the party, attorney, or agent that to the best of his or her knowledge the items of cost are correct and were necessarily incurred in the case. (Ibid.)

A party that fails to apply for costs within the time prescribed by rule 3.1700 waives those costs because the deadline for applying for costs, though not jurisdictional in the fundamental sense, is mandatory. (Hydratec, Inc. v. Sun Valley 260 Orchard & Vineyard Co. (1990) 223 Cal.App.3d 924, 929 (Hydratec) [“The time provisions relating to the filing of a memorandum of costs, while not jurisdictional, are mandatory”]; see, e.g., Sanabria v. Embrey (2001) 92 Cal.App.4th 422, 426 (Sanabria) [holding a trial court erred by granting untimely costs, citing Hydratec].)

b.     Parties’ Positions

Plaintiff’s initial argument against Defendant’s memorandum of costs is that the memo was untimely filed based on the Clerk’s service of notice of entry of judgment on October 31, 2025, and that California Rules of Court, rule 3.1700 requires service of the memorandum of costs within 15 days of notice of entry of judgment, plus additional days for service, rendering the memo untimely.

In opposition, Defendant argues that the 15-day rule in rule 3.1700 was never triggered because notice by the clerk on October 31, 2025, did not qualify as notice of entry of judgment or dismissal by the clerk under Code of Civil Procedure section 664.5. The opposition otherwise alludes but does not directly argue or cite authority for the position that rule 3.1700’s requirement that a memorandum of costs be filed within 15 days of “the date of service of written notice of entry of judgment or dismissal” is limited to notice of judgment or dismissal by a party, not the clerk.

No reply appears in the record.

c. Discussion

The Court finds Defendant has established that its Memorandum of Costs was timely filed and that Plaintiff has failed to demonstrate any basis for taxing the claimed costs.

(1) Timeliness of the Memorandum of Costs

California Rules of Court, rule 3.1700(a)(1) provides that a prevailing party claiming costs must serve and file a memorandum of costs within the earliest of: (1) 15 days after the date of service of the notice of entry of judgment or dismissal by the clerk under Code of Civil Procedure section 664.5; (2) 15 days after the date of service of written notice of entry of judgment or dismissal; or (3) 180 days after entry of judgment.

Plaintiff contends the Clerk's October 31, 2025 electronic notice of entry of judgment triggered the fifteen-day deadline because, even if it did not satisfy Code of Civil Procedure section 664.5, it nevertheless constituted "written notice of entry of judgment" within the meaning of the second triggering provision of rule 3.1700(a)(1). The Court disagrees.

As an initial matter, Defendant correctly argues that the Clerk's October 31, 2025 notice did not constitute notice of entry of judgment "under Code of Civil Procedure section 664.5." In Van Beurden Ins. Services, Inc. v. Customized Worldwide Weather Ins. Agency, Inc. (1997) 15 Cal.4th 51, 64, the California Supreme Court held that a clerk's notice qualifies as notice under section 664.5 only where it affirmatively states that it is given "upon order by the court" or "under section 664.5" and is accompanied by the requisite certificate of mailing. Subsequently, Simgel Co. v. Jaguar Land Rover North America, LLC (2020) 55 Cal.App.5th 305, 313-315, held that the Los Angeles Superior Court's standard LACIV-123 notice—which merely references section 664.5 in the footer—does not satisfy the requirements of section 664.5.

The October 31, 2025 notice at issue is the same form considered in Simgel. It does not affirmatively state that it was served pursuant to section 664.5 or by order of the Court. Accordingly, the Court concludes the Clerk's notice did not trigger the first fifteen-day deadline set forth in rule 3.1700(a)(1).

The Court further concludes that the Clerk's notice did not independently trigger the second fifteen-day deadline. Rule 3.1700(a)(1) identifies two separate fifteen-day triggering events: notice served by the clerk under Code of Civil Procedure section 664.5, and service of written notice of entry of judgment. Reading the second provision to encompass every written notice issued by the clerk—including notices that do not satisfy section 664.5—would substantially render the first provision meaningless by depriving the phrase "under Code of Civil Procedure section 664.5" of any operative effect. Statutes and rules must be construed to give significance to every word and to avoid interpretations that render language surplusage. (People v. Hudson (2006) 38 Cal.4th 1002, 1010.)

The more reasonable construction is that rule 3.1700 distinguishes between notice served by the clerk pursuant to section 664.5 and written notice served by a party. This interpretation gives effect to each triggering provision and is consistent with the structure of California's postjudgment procedural statutes. Plaintiff cites no published authority holding that a clerk's notice which fails to satisfy section 664.5 nevertheless constitutes "written notice of entry of judgment" for purposes of the second triggering provision. Likewise, Kahn v. Dewey Group (2015) 240 Cal.App.4th 227 merely addressed the computation of time following electronic service and did not consider whether a clerk's notice that fails to comply with section 664.5 nevertheless triggers the fifteen-day period.

Because the October 31, 2025 Clerk's notice did not qualify as notice under section 664.5, and because there is no evidence that any party served a written notice of entry of judgment, neither of the fifteen-day deadlines prescribed by rule 3.1700(a)(1) was triggered. Accordingly, Defendant was required only to file its Memorandum of Costs within 180 days after entry of judgment.

Judgment was entered on October 30, 2025. Defendant filed and served its Memorandum of Costs on April 23, 2026, well within 180 days after entry of judgment. The Memorandum of Costs was therefore timely.

(2) Reasonableness and Necessity of the Claimed Costs

Plaintiff alternatively argues that Defendant's Memorandum of Costs should be taxed because it fails to sufficiently itemize the claimed costs and does not establish that the costs were reasonable or necessary.

The argument is unpersuasive.

A verified memorandum of costs is prima facie evidence that the costs claimed were necessarily incurred. Where the items appear proper on their face, the burden rests on the party seeking to tax costs to demonstrate that a particular item is not recoverable, was not reasonably necessary to the litigation, or is unreasonable in amount. (Nelson v. Anderson (1999) 72 Cal.App.4th 111, 131; Ladas v. California State Auto. Assn. (1993) 19 Cal.App.4th 761, 774.)

Defendant filed its Memorandum of Costs on the mandatory Judicial Council form and verified it under penalty of perjury as required by California Rules of Court, rule 3.1700(a)(1). Plaintiff's assertion that Defendant was required to attach invoices or other supporting documentation to the Memorandum is contrary to established authority. A prevailing party is not required to submit bills, invoices, or receipts with its verified memorandum of costs. (Jones v. Dumrichob (1998) 63 Cal.App.4th 1258, 1267.) Rather, supporting documentation is generally required only after the costs have been challenged through a motion to tax costs. (Bach v. County of Butte (1989) 215 Cal.App.3d 294, 308.)

In response to Plaintiff's motion, Defendant submitted documentation identifying the filing fees and electronic filing charges comprising the requested $1,230.65. Plaintiff does not identify any particular charge that is unauthorized by statute, unnecessary to the litigation, or unreasonable in amount. Instead, Plaintiff advances only a generalized objection that Defendant's original Memorandum of Costs lacked sufficient detail.

Such a generalized objection is insufficient to overcome the evidentiary effect of a verified memorandum of costs. The filing fees and motion fees incurred in defending this action, including Defendant's first appearance fee and fees incurred in connection with its successful motion for summary judgment, are facially recoverable litigation costs under Code of Civil Procedure section 1033.5. Plaintiff has presented no evidence demonstrating that any specific cost was improperly incurred or unreasonable in amount. Accordingly, Plaintiff has failed to satisfy his burden of establishing that any portion of Defendant's claimed costs should be taxed.

d. Conclusion

Defendant timely filed and served its Memorandum of Costs within the period prescribed by California Rules of Court, rule 3.1700(a)(1). Plaintiff has further failed to demonstrate that any of Defendant's claimed costs were unauthorized, unreasonable, or unnecessary.

Accordingly, Plaintiff's Motion to Strike and/or Tax Defendant's Memorandum of Costs is DENIED.

Defendant shall recover costs in the amount of $1,230.65.

Plaintiff is ordered to give notice.

Case Number: 24STCV03912    Hearing Date: July 30, 2026    Dept: 731

[TENTATIVE] ORDER RE: DEFENDANT IMMCO INVESTMENT, LLC’S MOTION ESTABLISHING ADMISSIONS AND FOR MONETARY SANCTIONS IN THE AMOUNT OF $2250.00

Before the Court is Defendant Immco Investments, LLC’s (“Immco”) motion deeming as admitted the truth in request for admission served by Immco on in pro per Plaintiff, Eul Hyung Choi.

Immco served the motion on Plaintiff via mail to the address listed in her pleadings, as demonstrated by the proof of service attached to the notice of motion and motion, separate statement, declaration, and proposed order supporting the motion before the Court. (Compare Second Amended Complaint, p. 1 [identical physical address for Plaintiff], with June 3, 2026, filings [CRS No. 1408] [proofs of service showing service by mail at same address].)

No opposition appears in the record.

After review, the Court finds in favor of Immco.

A discovering party may file a motion to deem as admitted any unanswered requests for admission or any requests answered in a late or unverified response. (Code Civ. Proc., § 2033.280, subd. (b); see Code Civ. Proc., § 2033.240, subd. (a) [RFA responses must be signed by responding party under oath]; see Appleton v. Superior Court (1988) 206 Cal.App.3d 632, 636 [unsworn response to RFAs is treated like no response].) These requests are not automatically deemed admitted; the discovery party must make the motion. (See Code Civ. Proc., § 2033.280, subd. (b).)

To establish this ground, a movant must show (1) proper service (id. at § 2033.070), (2) expiration of the deadline to respond (id. at § 2033.250, subds. (a), (b)), and (3) that (a) the responding party served no response (Code Civ. Proc., § 2033.280, subd. (b)), (b) the propounding party served a late response (Code Civ. Proc., § 2033.280, subd. (b)), or (3) the responding party served an unsworn response (see Appleton v. Superior Court, supra, 206 Cal.App.3d at p. 636 [unsworn response to RFAs is treated like no response]).

Here, Immco’s paper’s show (1) proper service (see Jun. 3, 2026, filings [CRS No. 1408] at Proof of Service) and (2)-(3) nonresponse by Plaintiff after expiration of the response deadline (Motion, Garcia Decl., ¶¶ 3-7, Ex. A).

No opposition appears in the record to dispute this position.

Accordingly, Immco’s motion is GRANTED.

Immco also requests monetary sanctions. Code of Civil Procedure section 2033.280, subdivision (c), requires the Court to impose a monetary sanction against the party whose failure to serve timely responses necessitated the motion unless the Court finds that the party acted with substantial justification or that other circumstances make the imposition of sanctions unjust. No such showing has been made.

Accordingly, the request for monetary sanctions is GRANTED in the amount of $2,250.00, payable by Plaintiff Eul Hyung Choi to Defendant Immco Investments, LLC, through its counsel of record, within 30 days.

Defendant Immco Investments, LLC is ordered to give notice.
